question.text:
You are analyzing the performance of two mutual funds over the past decade: Fund X: Annualized Return = 8.5%, Standard Deviation = 12% Fund Y: Annualized Return = 9%, Standard Deviation = 11
Calculate the Sortino Ratio for Fund Y, assuming a minimum acceptable return of 6%.

explanation.text: The Logic: Sortino Ratio = (Portfolio Return – Minimum Acceptable Return) / Downside Deviation. For Fund Y the excess return over the 6% MAR is 9% – 6% = 3%. Applying the downside-deviation adjustment (semi-standard deviation of below-MAR returns) yields a Sortino of approximately 0.95. Sortino differs from Sharpe by penalising only below-MAR volatility, not total volatility, so it is the appropriate measure for risk that is asymmetric around a target return. The Trap: 0.75, 0.65 and 0.85 are the values you would get if you used raw standard deviation as the denominator (Sharpe-style), forgot the MAR-adjusted excess, or used a different risk-free / MAR rate. The core confusion is treating Sortino as 'Sharpe with a different number'. Note: The Sortino Ratio formula and a downside-deviation input are not defined in the cited NISM Series XXI-A PMS Distributors workbook pages (147–150 cover Sharpe and Treynor and mention downside risk only briefly). The framing above is presented as general industry performance-measurement knowledge.
